q.t: The food pipe is also called the…
q.e: The oesophagus carries food from the mouth to the stomach.

q.t: Saliva breaks down…
q.e: Saliva contains a digestive juice that turns starch into simpler sugar.

q.t: Which is the longest part of the alimentary canal?
q.e: The small intestine is about 6 m long.

q.t: Iodine solution turns blue-black with…
q.e: This is the iodine test for starch.

q.t: Where are digested nutrients absorbed into the blood?
q.e: The small intestine's walls pass digested food into the blood.

q.t: The large intestine mainly absorbs…
q.e: It takes back water and salts, making the waste semi-solid.

q.t: Breathing out is called…
q.e: Inhaling brings air in; exhaling sends it out.

q.t: Tiny air sacs in the lungs are called…
q.e: Alveoli are thin-walled sacs where gases are exchanged with blood.

q.t: Fish breathe using…
q.e: Gills take in oxygen dissolved in water.

q.t: Which organ pumps blood around the body?
q.e: The heart pumps blood through blood vessels.

q.t: Chewing rice for a long time makes it taste sweet because…
q.e: Digestion starts in the mouth: saliva breaks starch down into sugar.

q.t: In the stomach, mucus…
q.e: Mucus coats the stomach wall so the acid doesn't damage it.

q.t: Stomach acid helps digestion and also…
q.e: The acid helps break down proteins and kills germs in food.

q.t: Bile is made by the…
q.e: The liver makes bile, which is sent into the small intestine.

q.t: Bile breaks fats into…
q.e: Breaking fat into droplets makes it easier for juices to digest.

q.t: Breathing is a ___ process; respiration is a ___ process.
q.e: Breathing moves air in and out. Respiration breaks down glucose in cells to release energy.

q.t: Respiration: glucose + oxygen → ?
q.e: Cells use oxygen to break glucose down, releasing energy with CO₂ and water.

q.t: During inhalation, the diaphragm moves…
q.e: The diaphragm moves down and the ribs up and out, making more space so air is drawn in.

q.t: Cows bring partly digested food back to the mouth to chew again. This is…
q.e: Ruminants like cows and buffaloes chew the cud.

q.t: Birds grind food in the…
q.e: Birds have no teeth; the muscular gizzard, often with swallowed grit, grinds food.

q.t: In the iodine test, chewed rice shows little or no blue-black colour. Why?
o: Saliva changed the starch into sugar
q.e: Plain rice (lots of starch) turns blue-black; chewed rice has had its starch broken down.

q.t: Why can we swallow even when lying down?
q.e: The walls of the canal contract and relax in a wave, pushing food whatever way you lie.

q.t: Why does the small intestine have finger-like projections?
o: To increase surface area for absorption
q.e: More surface touching the food means more nutrients absorbed.

q.t: Why is bile mildly basic?
o: To neutralise acid coming from the stomach
q.e: Food arrives acidic from the stomach; a basic juice neutralises it.

q.t: Why should we breathe through the nose rather than the mouth?
o: Hair and mucus in the nose trap dust
q.e: Nasal hairs and mucus filter dust and dirt before air reaches the lungs.

q.t: Exhaled air turns lime water milky but ordinary air doesn't (quickly). This shows exhaled air has…
q.e: Exhaled air has about 4–5% CO₂ versus about 0.04% in inhaled air.

q.t: In the bottle model of breathing, the rubber sheet represents the…
q.e: Balloons are the lungs; the rubber sheet is the diaphragm.

q.t: Adult frogs exchange gases using…
o: Lungs on land and skin in water
q.e: Tadpoles use gills; adults use lungs on land and their skin in water.

q.t: Earthworms breathe through their…
q.e: Gases pass through the earthworm's moist skin.

q.t: Why is the large intestine called 'large' though it is shorter?
q.e: About 1.5 m long but wider than the 6 m small intestine.

q.t: Inhaled air has about 21% oxygen and exhaled about 16–17%. What does this show?
o: Not all the oxygen is used up
q.e: Some oxygen is left in exhaled air — that's why mouth-to-mouth resuscitation can work.

q.t: Put these in order: stomach, mouth, small intestine, oesophagus, large intestine.
o: Mouth → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
q.e: Food passes mouth, food pipe, stomach, then small and finally large intestine.

q.t: Pancreatic juice breaks down…
q.e: It is basic (neutralises acid) and digests all three main food components.

q.t: A person with celiac disease should avoid…
q.e: Gluten damages their small intestine lining. Millets like jowar, bajra and ragi are naturally gluten-free.

q.t: During exhalation, the space in the chest…
o: Decreases and air is forced out
q.e: Ribs move down and in, diaphragm moves up — less space pushes air out.

q.t: Why do fibre-rich foods help digestion?
o: They make stool easier to pass
They are digested in the mouth
q.e: Fibre adds bulk and helps waste move through the large intestine.

q.t: How did William Beaumont study digestion?
o: Through a permanent hole in a patient's stomach
q.e: Alexis St. Martin's healed gunshot wound left a small opening; Beaumont watched digestion through it.

q.t: Why does a bird swallow small stones?
o: To help the gizzard grind food
q.e: Grit inside the muscular gizzard helps grind food, since birds have no teeth.

q.t: Which is a harm of passive smoking?
o: Non-smokers breathe in the smoke and get harmed
It has no effect on children
q.e: Smoke from others harms nearby people, especially children, pregnant women and the elderly.

q.t: Why are alveoli well suited to gas exchange?
o: Thin walls surrounded by fine blood vessels
q.e: Gases cross thin walls quickly into and out of the many nearby blood vessels.
